gloss: Definite articles: le, la, les, l'
explanation: French nouns take a definite article that agrees in gender and number: le (masculine), la (feminine), les (plural). Before a vowel sound, le and la both shrink to l'. English drops "the" for general statements; French keeps it: j'aime le café.
Un (masculine) and une (feminine) mean "a"; des is the plural, "some", which English usually leaves out: j'ai des amis, I have friends.

gloss: Partitive articles: du, de la, de l'
explanation: For an unspecified quantity of something uncountable, French uses du, de la, or de l' where English says "some" or nothing: je bois du café. After a negation it collapses to de: je ne bois pas de café.

gloss: à + le = au, de + le = du
explanation: The prepositions à and de fuse with le and les: à + le = au, à + les = aux, de + le = du, de + les = des. They never fuse with la or l': à la gare, de l'hôtel.

gloss: Every noun is masculine or feminine
explanation: Each French noun has a fixed grammatical gender that has nothing to do with meaning. It decides which article, adjective ending, and pronoun go with it, so learn the article with the noun: une table, un livre.

Most nouns form the plural by adding a silent -s, so the article carries the sound of the plural: le livre / les livres. Nouns ending in -eau or -al change instead: bateau → bateaux, journal → journaux.

gloss: Adjectives agree in gender and number
explanation: Adjectives change ending to match their noun: petit, petite, petits, petites. The feminine usually adds -e, which often makes a silent final consonant audible: grand /grã/ → grande /grãd/.
Unlike English, most French adjectives come after the noun: une voiture rouge. A small set of short, common ones go before: beau, bon, grand, petit, jeune, vieux, nouveau, mauvais.
Possessive adjectives agree with the thing owned, not the owner: mon livre, ma maison, mes amis. Before a feminine noun starting with a vowel, ma becomes mon: mon amie.
Ce (masculine), cet (masculine before a vowel), cette (feminine), and ces (plural) all mean "this" or "that"; French does not distinguish near from far unless you add -ci or -là: ce livre-là.

gloss: Subject pronouns: je, tu, il/elle, nous, vous, ils/elles
explanation: French verbs always need a stated subject pronoun. Je shrinks to j' before a vowel. Ils covers any group that includes a masculine noun; elles is for all-feminine groups.
Tu addresses one person you are close to; vous addresses a group, or one person politely. Shopkeepers, strangers, and most adults you have just met get vous. The verb ending changes with the choice.
In everyday speech on replaces nous as "we" and takes the same verb form as il: on va au marché. It also means "one" or "people in general": on dit que...
Drop -er and add -e, -es, -e, -ons, -ez, -ent: je parle, tu parles, il parle, nous parlons, vous parlez, ils parlent. Four of the six forms sound identical; the spelling changes are silent.
Drop -ir and add -is, -is, -it, -issons, -issez, -issent: je finis, nous finissons. The plural forms insert -iss-.
Drop -re and add -s, -s, nothing, -ons, -ez, -ent: je vends, il vend, nous vendons.

gloss: Irregular present: être, avoir, aller, faire
explanation: The four most common verbs are irregular and must be memorised: je suis / j'ai / je vais / je fais. They also build other tenses, so they are worth knowing cold.

Negation wraps the conjugated verb: je ne sais pas. In speech the ne is often dropped, leaving just pas after the verb: je sais pas. Other pairs work the same way: ne... jamais, ne... rien, ne... plus.
Put est-ce que in front of a statement to make a neutral question without changing word order: est-ce que tu viens? Question words go before it: où est-ce que tu vas?
In more formal French the verb and subject pronoun swap and are joined by a hyphen: viens-tu? A -t- is inserted between two vowels: a-t-il?
In conversation, a statement with rising intonation is the most common question form: tu viens? No word-order change at all.
The everyday past tense is a present form of avoir plus a past participle: j'ai mangé, tu as fini, il a vendu. Regular participles end in -é, -i, -u.

A short list of movement and change-of-state verbs (aller, venir, arriver, partir, rester, naître, mourir...) and all reflexive verbs use être instead of avoir, and the participle agrees with the subject: elle est allée.

The imparfait describes what was going on, used to happen, or how things were: il faisait beau, je jouais souvent. Take the nous form of the present, drop -ons, add -ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient.
A present form of aller followed by an infinitive expresses what is about to happen, like English "going to": je vais manger. It is the everyday future in speech.
The conditional softens a request, like English "would": je voudrais un café rather than je veux. It is built from the future stem plus the imparfait endings: voudr- + -ais.
Commands use the tu, nous, or vous form without the pronoun: écoute, écoutons, écoutez. For -er verbs the tu form drops its -s: parle! Object pronouns attach after with a hyphen: excusez-moi.
Many daily-routine verbs take a reflexive pronoun that matches the subject: je me lève, tu te lèves, il se lève. In the passé composé they use être: je me suis levé.

gloss: Direct object pronouns before the verb
explanation: Me, te, le, la, nous, vous, les replace a direct object and go before the conjugated verb, not after it as in English: je le vois, I see him / it.
Lui (to him / to her) and leur (to them) replace à + person and sit before the verb: je lui parle, I am talking to him.
Y replaces à + a place or thing and goes before the verb: tu vas à Paris? j'y vais. It is why on y va means "let's go (there)".
En replaces de + something, often a quantity: tu veux du pain? j'en veux. It sits before the verb and is required even when English says nothing.

gloss: Il y a: there is / there are
explanation: Il y a is invariable and means both "there is" and "there are": il y a un problème, il y a des gens. With a time expression it means "ago": il y a deux ans.
Il faut plus an infinitive says what must be done in general: il faut partir. Il followed by a noun means something is needed: il faut du temps.
Use c'est before a noun with an article or a pronoun: c'est un ami, c'est moi. Use il est or elle est before an adjective or a bare profession: il est médecin, elle est contente.
Age, hunger, thirst, fear, and being right use avoir, not être: j'ai vingt ans, j'ai faim, tu as raison. Because faim is a noun, everyday speech intensifies it with très: j'ai très faim.
French has no -ing form; to stress that something is happening right now, use être en train de plus an infinitive: je suis en train de lire. Otherwise the plain present already covers it.
Compare with plus (more), moins (less), or aussi (as) before the adjective and que after it: elle est plus grande que moi. Bon becomes meilleur, not plus bon.
Dans (in), sur (on), sous (under), devant (in front of), derrière (behind), entre (between), à côté de (next to), en face de (opposite). Those ending in de contract with le and les: à côté du parc.
Elision drops a final vowel before another vowel: je + ai = j'ai, le + homme = l'homme. Liaison sounds a normally silent final consonant when the next word begins with a vowel: les_amis, vous_avez.
